title: Race Day Setup for Inline Speed Skating: What to Check a Week, a Night and an Hour Before
thumbnail_text: Races are lost in the pits, not the legs

scenes.heading: Race Day Setup for Inline Speed Skating
scenes.sub: What to check a week, a night and an hour before
scenes.chapter: Why races are lost in the pits
scenes.narration: This is a simple race day routine for inline speed skaters. You will learn what to check in race week, the night before, and in the last hour before your start. Most skaters train hard for months, then lose time through preparation, not fitness. A bolt works loose in the warm up. The wheel choice is wrong for the surface. The bearings were stripped the night before and never settled. None of this is dramatic. But every one of these costs you on race day, and every one is avoidable.

scenes.heading: One rule for race day
bullets: Race day is not the day to try anything new
Race only on kit you have skated on
Make a known setup reliable
Push every decision as early as possible
scenes.narration: One rule runs through this whole routine. Race day is not the day to try anything new. Everything you race on should be something you have already skated on. Preparation is about making a known setup reliable. It is not about making it different. So the plan follows the way a race weekend actually unfolds. There is race week, the night before, and the hour before your start. The idea is to push every decision as early as you can. That way race day is only about checking, never about choosing.

scenes.heading: When to do what
scenes.narration: Here is the whole routine on one line. In race week, you confirm your wheel choice, clean and oil your bearings, and skate on the setup. The night before, you check every bolt, rotate wheels if they need it, and pack the bag fully. In the hour before, you spin each wheel and listen, feel the actual surface, and get your suit on with your laces set. And one line sits under all of it. Nothing new goes on the skate after race week closes.

scenes.heading: Race week: change it or leave it
bullets: Change: worn, broken or wrong for the venue
Leave: frame position, heat moulding, lacing
Leave: bearings that spin clean
Leave: a suit that already fits
scenes.chapter: Race week: change it or leave it
scenes.narration: The most common mistake in race week is change. New wheels, new bearings, a new frame position, a suit you have never worn. Each one adds an unknown right when you want none. If something really needs replacing, do it early, so you get two or three sessions on it first. Here is a simple test. Change something only if it is worn out, broken, or clearly wrong for the venue. A wheel with a chunk out of it, a bearing that grinds, a frayed lace or a cracked strap all qualify. Leave it alone if the only reason to touch it is nerves. Frame position, boot heat moulding and your lacing pattern take sessions to adapt to, not hours. Bearings that spin freely and sound clean can stay as they are.

scenes.heading: Grip against roll
scenes.narration: Wheel firmness is the one setting that really should change with the venue. Many skaters think harder is always faster. On a rough or dusty surface, that is often true. But on a hard, smooth, dry track, a wheel that is too hard starts to slide instead of holding your line through the corner. And slip costs far more than a small difference in roll. This diagram shows the trade. An XFirm wheel, at 84 to 86A, is softer and grips better on hard, smooth, dry surfaces. An XXFirm wheel, at 86 to 88A, gives more roll and outright speed when the surface allows it. Dust, damp and tight corners all favour grip. Long straights favour roll. And if you are unsure, race the wheel you trained on, because confidence in the corner is worth more than a gain on paper.

scenes.heading: Bearings: clean and settled
bullets: Service early in race week
Clean and dry fully before oiling
One drop of oil per bearing
Skate on them before you race
scenes.narration: Bearings are the classic race day mistake. Skaters strip and oil a full set the night before. Then the wheels feel heavy and noisy for the first few laps, because nothing has bedded in and there is too much oil in the races. Service them early in race week instead, and skate on them at least once before you race. If they are dirty, clean them and let them dry completely, because oil binds to grit. Then add one drop of oil per bearing, spin it by hand to spread it, and wipe off the excess. One drop is the sweet spot. A flooded bearing collects dust and drags. And remember the numbers. A pair of four wheel skates runs sixteen bearings, so a spare or two in the bag is cheap insurance.

scenes.heading: The night before: hardware
bullets: Every axle tight, no side play
Frame mounting bolts on both skates
Spin each wheel and listen
Check wear, laces, buckles and straps
scenes.narration: The night before is a mechanical job, not a performance one. Work through each skate in order. Check that every axle is tight and that no wheel has side to side play. Check the frame mounting bolts on both skates, because these loosen slowly and silently. Spin each wheel and listen. A rough or rattly bearing should tell you tonight, not during the race. Look across the wheels for uneven wear, and rotate if one is clearly further gone. Then check your laces, buckles and straps for fraying and cracks. Snug each frame bolt firmly without leaning on the key. And if you moved your frame recently, confirm it is where you expect. Frame position drift is easy to miss on the bench, and you feel it straight away off the line.

scenes.heading: What goes in the bag
scenes.narration: Pack the bag the night before, not in the morning. A checklist beats memory when you are nervous and short of sleep. This layout splits it into four groups. Skate kit: your skates with race wheels fitted, a second wheel set, your helmet and spare laces. Tools and spares: allen keys, bearing oil, spare bearings, spare axles and a clean cloth. Race clothing: your skin suit, warm layers, spare socks, gloves and a dry change of kit. And fuel and admin: water, simple food, race numbers, your licence and ID, and the start list times. Check it against the list once in the morning, and you are done.

scenes.heading: Your suit is equipment
bullets: Dry, uncreased and already familiar
Wear it in training first
Suit on before final skate checks
Warm layer over it, dry change after
scenes.narration: Your race suit belongs on the list too, because it is equipment, not just clothing. It should be dry, uncreased, and already familiar on your body. A suit that binds across the shoulders or rides at the knee changes how you sit in the low position. So wear it in training before you race in it, and never open a new suit on the start line. Put it on before your final skate checks, so you are not fighting a zip with cold hands. Have a warm layer to pull over it while you wait. And carry a dry change for after the race, so you spend the next week training, not ill.

scenes.heading: The final hour
scenes.narration: By the last hour, nothing should need fixing. This hour is for confirming, warming up and staying calm. At sixty minutes, spin each wheel and listen, and check the axles and frame bolts after the trip in the bag. At forty five minutes, do an easy skate on the race surface and read the grip, so your first contact with it is not the first corner of the race. At twenty five minutes, get your suit on with a warm layer over it, and set your laces the way you always do. At fifteen minutes, do your activation and short efforts, and sip water. Then put the tools away, breathe, and race the plan. If you are still holding an allen key at fifteen minutes, something went wrong last night.

scenes.heading: Between heats and after
bullets: Wipe grit off, stay warm, drink
Only touch skates if something changed
After: wipe down, check for damaged wheels
Gritty bearings? Service early next race week
scenes.chapter: Between heats and after the race
scenes.narration: If you race more than one distance, keep the routine between heats short and repeatable. Wipe the grit off the wheels, keep warm and drink. Only touch the skates if something has actually changed. Fiddling between rounds is almost always a mistake. After the race, take ten minutes to protect your kit. Wipe the wheels and frames down, especially after a dusty or damp surface. Look for any wheel that took a chunk out in the pack. Loosen the laces, let the boots air, and do not leave a damp suit balled up in the bag. If your bearings sounded gritty, note it, and service them early in the next race week.

scenes.heading: Nothing new after race week closes
scenes.sub: Full guide at livelica.com, link in the description
scenes.narration: If you remember one thing, make it this. Nothing new goes on the skate after race week closes. Decide early, check late, and let the last fifteen minutes belong to your legs and your head. The single most overlooked check is the frame mounting bolts, so check them the night before every race. The full guide, with the complete checklists and answers to common questions, is on the LiveLica blog. The link is in the description.
